chapterTitle: Troubleshooting Network Services (DHCP, DNS, NTP, AAA)
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 12-minute live coding video demonstrating troubleshooting of network services on a Cisco IOS-XE router. Start with a scenario where DHCP clients are not getting IPs, show missing `ip helper-address`, add it, and verify with `debug ip dhcp relay`. Then, show a DNS resolution failure, demonstrate `nslookup` from the router, add `ip name-server`, and re-test. Finally, show an unsynchronized clock, configure `ntp server`, and verify with `show ntp status`. Use a split-screen view for CLI and a simple network diagram. Emphasize the importance of `debug` commands and their careful use. Include a mini-quiz on common misconfigurations for each service.

---

screens.title: Troubleshooting Network Services
screens.narratorSegment: Network services are often invisible until they fail. In this chapter you will learn a disciplined way to find root causes for DHCP address failures, DNS resolution problems, NTP clock drift, and AAA authentication errors. We will emphasize a repeatable workflow: confirm basic IP reachability, validate local configuration, inspect server-side state, and then use targeted show and debug commands to observe protocol exchanges. You will also see common misconfigurations — missing ip helper-address, wrong name-server entries, blocked UDP ports, or a shared-secret mismatch — and learn safe practices so you don’t lock yourself out when changing AAA settings. A practical branch-office scenario will tie these checks together with concrete IOS commands to verify and fix issues. By the end of this lesson you will understand not just what commands to run, but why each step matters and how to interpret the output. Think about the last time a service outage disrupted users: this chapter gives you the checklist and the commands to resolve it efficiently.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Troubleshooting Network Services
Troubleshooting Network Services
DHCP, DNS, NTP, and AAA are foundational. This lesson gives you inspection steps, IOS show/debug commands, and safe practices to resolve failures quickly and correctly.
In this lesson
A structured checklist, common IOS commands, and a hands-on branch scenario to practice fixes safely.
Why it matters
Addressing, name resolution, time sync, and access control are prerequisites for reliable services and secure operations.
Coming up: DHCP relay checks, DNS server validation, NTP associations, AAA server tests, and safe debug practices.
Service Map
DHCP ↔ DNS ↔ NTP ↔ AAA
Connections show common failure propagation: an IP problem can mask DNS and AAA failures.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
DHCP
Pool, bindings, helper-address, relay debugging.
DNS
Client name-server, server zones, port 53 path checks.
NTP
Associations, reachability, authenticated keys.
AAA
Method lists, shared secrets, test commands.
Explore Key Topics
Debug safely
Use debug selectively and maintain console access to avoid lockouts.
Check reachability
Ping and trace basic IP connectivity before diving into service configs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives lay out the practical skills you will build. First, you will diagnose DHCP failures by checking client behavior, server pools, and relay configuration while using show and debug tools to surface protocol exchanges. Second, you will troubleshoot DNS by validating client name-server settings, exercising nslookup, and confirming server zone health while watching for blocked port 53 paths. Third, you will identify and correct NTP synchronization issues, learn to read ntp associations, and detect authentication key mismatches or firewall blocks. Fourth, you will debug AAA failures by verifying reachability, checking shared secrets, confirming method lists, and using test commands to validate credentials. Each objective emphasizes why the step matters and how it prevents wider outages. You will also practice safe debugging so that critical devices remain accessible while you gather necessary diagnostic output. These goals will prepare you to resolve service outages reliably and to interpret IOS outputs with confidence.

You will learn to use specific show commands to inspect protocol state, such as show ip dhcp pool, show ip dhcp binding, show hosts, show ntp status, and show ntp associations detail. screens.title: A Repeatable Troubleshooting Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Before running any command, adopt a structured workflow. First, confirm basic IP connectivity: ping the server from the gateway and from the device that reports the issue. This rules out routing and ACL problems. Second, validate local configuration: on the client check that DHCP is enabled, or that the named servers are configured. Third, inspect server-side state with targeted show commands to see available resources, bindings, and associations. Fourth, use precise debug commands to watch the protocol exchange only when you need packet-level visibility. For example, if DHCP fails, ping the DHCP server, check the SVI or interface configuration for ip helper-address, view show ip dhcp pool to confirm available addresses, and then enable debug ip dhcp relay to observe a Discover being forwarded. A common misconception is to jump immediately to changing server settings; instead, confirm reachability and config precedence first. This workflow reduces time-to-repair and avoids disruptive, unnecessary changes. A Repeatable Troubleshooting Workflow means confirm reachability, validate local config, inspect server state, and debug selectively — repeat for each service in turn.. In practical terms, a four-step checklist to find root cause quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › Troubleshooting Workflow
1. Confirm reachability
Ping servers, check routes, and ensure ACLs are not blocking required UDP/TCP ports before changing service configs.
2. Validate local config
Verify client or interface settings such as DHCP enablement, ip helper-address, and ip name-server entries.
3. Inspect server state
Use show commands to check pools, bindings, zone records, NTP associations, and AAA server reachability/logs.
4. Debug selectively
Run targeted debug commands to observe exchanges; avoid broad debugs on production devices without console access.
Key Takeaway

A systematic approach prevents wasted effort and reduces risk. Always confirm reachability before changing service parameters.

Example Walkthrough
Problem: Clients fail DHCP. Apply the checklist to determine if it's interface, relay, or server-side.
Checks & Commands
  • Ping DHCP server from gateway: ping 172.16.1.10
  • Verify interface config: show running-config interface Vlan10
  • Inspect pool: show ip dhcp pool
  • Debug relay if needed: debug ip dhcp relay

screens.title: DHCP Fundamentals for Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding DHCP operations helps you pinpoint where an address assignment fails. DHCP relies on the client sending a broadcast Discover, a relay optionally forwarding that as unicast, the server selecting an address from a pool, and then the offer-request-ack sequence. When troubleshooting, first confirm the client is set to obtain an address automatically and that its interface is operational. If the server is remote, verify the router SVI has an ip helper-address pointing at the DHCP server and that the helper is configured on the correct interface. On the server side, inspect the pool configuration with show ip dhcp pool to ensure the network and default-router are correct, and use show ip dhcp binding to confirm existing leases. A common misconception is that an available pool guarantees assignment; exhaustion or excluded addresses can still prevent assignment. Finally, remember UDP 67/68 must traverse without ACL drops. Thinking in terms of client, relay, and server clarifies where to focus commands and prevents chasing the wrong device. DHCP Fundamentals for Troubleshooting means treat dhcp problems as client, relay, or server issues and test each element with targeted commands.. In practical terms, what to verify on client, server, and relay agent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › DHCP Troubleshooting
Client checks
Ensure DHCP is enabled on the host, interface is up, and the client can broadcast. If static works but DHCP does not, the client config or network path is suspect.
Server checks
Confirm pool, default-router, DNS, and free addresses with show ip dhcp pool and show ip dhcp binding; check server reachability with ping.
Relay agent
Validate ip helper-address on the correct SVI or interface and ensure UDP ports 67/68 are permitted through ACLs.
Concrete example
If VLAN 10 clients do not get addresses, check the Vlan10 SVI config. Missing ip helper-address is a frequent culprit when the DHCP server is on another subnet.
Common-mistake
Configuring helper-address on the wrong interface or forgetting to add it entirely causes Discover messages to never reach the server.
Key Takeaway

Think in client, relay, server steps and test each with show/debug commands to isolate the failure domain.

screens.title: DHCP Server and IOS Commands
screens.narratorSegment: When diagnosing server-side DHCP state, use show commands to read configuration, pool allocations, and conflicts. show ip dhcp pool reveals pool definitions, network statements, default-router, DNS settings, and how many addresses are in use. show ip dhcp binding lists leases the server has issued so you can verify that particular client MACs received an address. show ip dhcp conflict helps find duplicate addresses or conflicts. On IOS devices acting as servers, show ip dhcp server statistics indicates whether the service is running and tallies packets. Use show running-config interface to confirm ip helper-address placement on relays. A misconception is assuming the pool exists and is sufficient; pools can be mis-scoped or exhausted. content.html:
Process Flow › DHCP Server Commands
When to run these
Run show ip dhcp pool to confirm pool parameters, then show ip dhcp binding to check lease assignments. Use show ip dhcp conflict if duplicates are suspected.
Supporting points
  • Pool misconfiguration can set the wrong default-router or DNS.
  • Bindings show MAC-to-IP mapping; absence indicates the server never assigned a lease.
  • Conflicts can prevent assignment even when addresses appear available.
Command examples
show ip dhcp pool
show ip dhcp binding
show ip dhcp conflict
show ip dhcp server statistics
show running-config interface Vlan10
Use these in order: pool → binding → conflict → server stats. If the pool shows few free addresses, investigate exclusions or scope errors.
Common-mistake

Assuming the server is reachable; always ping the server from the gateway before deeper server checks.

screens.title: DHCP Relay (ip helper-address) Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: The DHCP relay agent, commonly configured with ip helper-address on a VLAN SVI or routed interface, forwards client broadcast messages to a remote DHCP server. Many production incidents stem from the helper address being absent or applied to the wrong interface. When the client and server are on different subnets, the router handling the client-subnet must receive the broadcast and translate it as a unicast to the server. If you configure the helper on a different SVI, discovers never reach the relay. Also check for ACLs that may block UDP ports 67 and 68 between the relay and server. Use show running-config interface Vlan10 to confirm the helper entry and debug ip dhcp relay to watch discover packets being forwarded. Remember to remove or limit debug output after collecting evidence to avoid excessive console noise. A good troubleshooting habit is to test with a ping to the server from the SVI, then enable relay debugging to confirm the Discover turning into a unicast toward the server IP. DHCP Relay (ip helper-address) Deep Dive means ip helper-address must be on the client-facing interface and udp 67/68 must be allowed; otherwise discover packets never reach the server.. In practical terms, why helper placement and acls matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › DHCP Relay Agent
What to verify
Ping the DHCP server from the SVI, confirm the helper address on that interface, and check ACLs for UDP 67/68.
Quick checklist
  • show running-config interface Vlan10
  • ping 172.16.1.10 source Vlan10
  • debug ip dhcp relay
Example scenario
VLAN 10 clients cannot obtain leases. show running-config shows no ip helper-address on Vlan10. Adding ip helper-address 172.16.1.10 and testing with debug ip dhcp relay shows Discover forwarded and leases issue.
Pro tip
If multiple helper-address entries are needed for different servers, list them explicitly. Verify reachability to each before assuming relay is fault-free.

screens.title: DNS Resolution Failure Modes
screens.narratorSegment: DNS failures commonly fall into two categories: client-side misconfiguration and server-side resolution or zone issues. On the client side, make sure the host receives correct DNS server IPs either via DHCP or static configuration. Confirm the client can ping the DNS server and then use nslookup or dig to query a hostname directly against the server. If the client receives accurate DNS server entries but nslookup fails, move to the DNS server: ensure the service listens on UDP/TCP 53, check zones for the queried name, and test resolution with nslookup hostname dns_server_ip. Network path issues are frequent — firewalls or ACLs may block port 53 between the client and server or between the DNS server and upstream resolvers. On Cisco devices, ip domain-lookup and ip name-server entries govern router behavior for name resolution. A misconception is to assume DNS always fails because of the server; often a simple ACL or wrong name-server entry handed out by DHCP is the root cause. DNS Resolution Failure Modes means distinguish client name-server misconfiguration from server or network-path problems and test each with nslookup and port checks.. In practical terms, client misconfiguration vs server-side problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › DNS Troubleshooting
Client-side checks
Confirm client has correct DNS server IPs, can ping the server, and run nslookup to verify resolution or error messages.
Server-side checks
Ensure DNS service is listening on port 53, zones contain the expected records, and the server can resolve upstream names if recursive queries are required.
Network path
Look for firewall or ACL blocks on UDP/TCP 53. Also verify that intermediate devices do not accidentally redirect or filter DNS traffic.
Concrete example
Clients receive DNS server 172.16.1.10 via DHCP but nslookup to that IP times out. A firewall was blocking UDP 53 between the branch and the server.
Key Takeaway

Use nslookup against a specific DNS server to separate client configuration issues from server or path problems.

screens.title: DNS on Cisco IOS — Router Checks and Commands
screens.narratorSegment: On Cisco routers, a few global commands determine how the device performs name resolution. ip domain-lookup enables on-box DNS name resolution; without it the router will not attempt to resolve names received from users or applications. ip name-server entries point the router at one or more DNS servers. Use show hosts to view local host entries and cached records. If end-users report inability to resolve, verify the router's ip name-server points at a reachable DNS server and then test resolution using nslookup or debug domain to observe queries. Remember port considerations: UDP 53 is primary, but TCP 53 is used for larger responses and zone transfers. A common misconception is that routers automatically inherit DNS servers from clients; the router only uses its configured name-server entries. When DNS is failing for clients, confirm the DHCP-based name-server distribution and the router's own ability to forward or resolve names as necessary. DNS on Cisco IOS — Router Checks and Commands means ensure ip domain-lookup is enabled and ip name-server entries point to reachable dns servers; use debug domain for query visibility.. In practical terms, ip domain-lookup, ip name-server, and debug domain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Cisco DNS Commands
Commands to verify
ip domain-lookup
ip name-server 172.16.1.10
show hosts
debug domain
nslookup www.example.com 172.16.1.10
Run nslookup against the DNS server IP to check authoritative answers and to separate router issues from DNS server problems.
Supporting explanation
If ip domain-lookup is disabled, the router will not attempt name resolution. Ensure ip name-server list is current and reachable from the router.
Concrete example

fullNarratorScript:
Network services are often invisible until they fail. In this chapter you will learn a disciplined way to find root causes for DHCP address failures, DNS resolution problems, NTP clock drift, and AAA authentication errors. We will emphasize a repeatable workflow: confirm basic IP reachability, validate local configuration, inspect server-side state, and then use targeted show and debug commands to observe protocol exchanges. You will also see common misconfigurations — missing ip helper-address, wrong name-server entries, blocked UDP ports, or a shared-secret mismatch — and learn safe practices so you don’t lock yourself out when changing AAA settings. A practical branch-office scenario will tie these checks together with concrete IOS commands to verify and fix issues. By the end of this lesson you will understand not just what commands to run, but why each step matters and how to interpret the output. Think about the last time a service outage disrupted users: this chapter gives you the checklist and the commands to resolve it efficiently.

These objectives lay out the practical skills you will build. First, you will diagnose DHCP failures by checking client behavior, server pools, and relay configuration while using show and debug tools to surface protocol exchanges. Second, you will troubleshoot DNS by validating client name-server settings, exercising nslookup, and confirming server zone health while watching for blocked port 53 paths. Third, you will identify and correct NTP synchronization issues, learn to read ntp associations, and detect authentication key mismatches or firewall blocks. Fourth, you will debug AAA failures by verifying reachability, checking shared secrets, confirming method lists, and using test commands to validate credentials. Each objective emphasizes why the step matters and how it prevents wider outages. You will also practice safe debugging so that critical devices remain accessible while you gather necessary diagnostic output. These goals will prepare you to resolve service outages reliably and to interpret IOS outputs with confidence.

These secondary objectives focus on tooling and safety. You will learn to use specific show commands to inspect protocol state, such as show ip dhcp pool, show ip dhcp binding, show hosts, show ntp status, and show ntp associations detail. You will learn which debug commands provide the needed packet-level visibility and when they are safe to run: debug ip dhcp server packet, debug ip dhcp relay, debug domain, debug ntp packet, and debug aaa authentication. You will also practice common-mistake recognition: ACLs blocking UDP 67/68 or 53, missing ip helper-address on the wrong interface, shared-secret mismatches, and forgetting ntp authenticate keys. Finally, you will adopt safe change patterns: include a local fallback in AAA method lists and retain console access before enabling debug. Mastering these skills reduces mean time to repair and avoids accidental lockouts during live troubleshooting.

Before running any command, adopt a structured workflow. First, confirm basic IP connectivity: ping the server from the gateway and from the device that reports the issue. This rules out routing and ACL problems. Second, validate local configuration: on the client check that DHCP is enabled, or that the named servers are configured. Third, inspect server-side state with targeted show commands to see available resources, bindings, and associations. Fourth, use precise debug commands to watch the protocol exchange only when you need packet-level visibility. For example, if DHCP fails, ping the DHCP server, check the SVI or interface configuration for ip helper-address, view show ip dhcp pool to confirm available addresses, and then enable debug ip dhcp relay to observe a Discover being forwarded. A common misconception is to jump immediately to changing server settings; instead, confirm reachability and config precedence first. This workflow reduces time-to-repair and avoids disruptive, unnecessary changes. A Repeatable Troubleshooting Workflow means confirm reachability, validate local config, inspect server state, and debug selectively — repeat for each service in turn.. In practical terms, a four-step checklist to find root cause quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding DHCP operations helps you pinpoint where an address assignment fails. DHCP relies on the client sending a broadcast Discover, a relay optionally forwarding that as unicast, the server selecting an address from a pool, and then the offer-request-ack sequence. When troubleshooting, first confirm the client is set to obtain an address automatically and that its interface is operational. If the server is remote, verify the router SVI has an ip helper-address pointing at the DHCP server and that the helper is configured on the correct interface. On the server side, inspect the pool configuration with show ip dhcp pool to ensure the network and default-router are correct, and use show ip dhcp binding to confirm existing leases. A common misconception is that an available pool guarantees assignment; exhaustion or excluded addresses can still prevent assignment. Finally, remember UDP 67/68 must traverse without ACL drops. Thinking in terms of client, relay, and server clarifies where to focus commands and prevents chasing the wrong device. DHCP Fundamentals for Troubleshooting means treat dhcp problems as client, relay, or server issues and test each element with targeted commands.. In practical terms, what to verify on client, server, and relay agent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When diagnosing server-side DHCP state, use show commands to read configuration, pool allocations, and conflicts. show ip dhcp pool reveals pool definitions, network statements, default-router, DNS settings, and how many addresses are in use. show ip dhcp binding lists leases the server has issued so you can verify that particular client MACs received an address. show ip dhcp conflict helps find duplicate addresses or conflicts. On IOS devices acting as servers, show ip dhcp server statistics indicates whether the service is running and tallies packets. Use show running-config interface to confirm ip helper-address placement on relays. A misconception is assuming the pool exists and is sufficient; pools can be mis-scoped or exhausted. The following code block provides the essential commands you will run repeatedly while diagnosing DHCP server problems. DHCP Server and IOS Commands means show ip dhcp pool, show ip dhcp binding, show ip dhcp conflict, and show ip dhcp server statistics reveal server capacity and state.. In practical terms, key show commands to understand server state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The DHCP relay agent, commonly configured with ip helper-address on a VLAN SVI or routed interface, forwards client broadcast messages to a remote DHCP server. Many production incidents stem from the helper address being absent or applied to the wrong interface. When the client and server are on different subnets, the router handling the client-subnet must receive the broadcast and translate it as a unicast to the server. If you configure the helper on a different SVI, discovers never reach the relay. Also check for ACLs that may block UDP ports 67 and 68 between the relay and server. Use show running-config interface Vlan10 to confirm the helper entry and debug ip dhcp relay to watch discover packets being forwarded. Remember to remove or limit debug output after collecting evidence to avoid excessive console noise. A good troubleshooting habit is to test with a ping to the server from the SVI, then enable relay debugging to confirm the Discover turning into a unicast toward the server IP. DHCP Relay (ip helper-address) Deep Dive means ip helper-address must be on the client-facing interface and udp 67/68 must be allowed; otherwise discover packets never reach the server.. In practical terms, why helper placement and acls matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DNS failures commonly fall into two categories: client-side misconfiguration and server-side resolution or zone issues. On the client side, make sure the host receives correct DNS server IPs either via DHCP or static configuration. Confirm the client can ping the DNS server and then use nslookup or dig to query a hostname directly against the server. If the client receives accurate DNS server entries but nslookup fails, move to the DNS server: ensure the service listens on UDP/TCP 53, check zones for the queried name, and test resolution with nslookup hostname dns_server_ip. Network path issues are frequent — firewalls or ACLs may block port 53 between the client and server or between the DNS server and upstream resolvers. On Cisco devices, ip domain-lookup and ip name-server entries govern router behavior for name resolution. A misconception is to assume DNS always fails because of the server; often a simple ACL or wrong name-server entry handed out by DHCP is the root cause. DNS Resolution Failure Modes means distinguish client name-server misconfiguration from server or network-path problems and test each with nslookup and port checks.. In practical terms, client misconfiguration vs server-side problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

On Cisco routers, a few global commands determine how the device performs name resolution. ip domain-lookup enables on-box DNS name resolution; without it the router will not attempt to resolve names received from users or applications. ip name-server entries point the router at one or more DNS servers. Use show hosts to view local host entries and cached records. If end-users report inability to resolve, verify the router's ip name-server points at a reachable DNS server and then test resolution using nslookup or debug domain to observe queries. Remember port considerations: UDP 53 is primary, but TCP 53 is used for larger responses and zone transfers. A common misconception is that routers automatically inherit DNS servers from clients; the router only uses its configured name-server entries. When DNS is failing for clients, confirm the DHCP-based name-server distribution and the router's own ability to forward or resolve names as necessary.
